Garsia–Remmel qq-rook numbers
are not always unimodal

Joel Brewster Lewis Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, George Washington University
jblewis@gwu.edu    Alejandro H. Morales Note: corresponding author Affiliation: LACIM, Département de Mathématiques, Université du Québec à Montréal
ahmorales.math@gmail.com
September 2025
Abstract

We show by an explicit example that the Garsia–Remmel qq-rook numbers of Ferrers boards do not all have unimodal sequences of coefficients. This resolves in the negative a question from 1986 by the aforementioned authors.

Dedicated to the memory of Adriano Garsia.

keywords: qq-rook numbers, rook placements, Ferrers boards, unimodality, counterexamples, q-Stirling numbers

The central objects in rook theory are the placements of (nonattacking) rooks on a board. Formally, a board BB is a finite subset of ℤ>0×ℤ>0\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\times\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, and a rook placement on BB is a subset ww of BB such that no two elements of ww agree on either coordinate. The terminology comes from the natural visual representation of these objects, as in Figure 1. The rook number Rr​(B)R_{r}(B) is defined as the number of placements of rr rooks on the board BB.

A case of particular interest (beginning in the first systematic study [20] of the field) is when B=BλB=B_{\lambda} is a Ferrers board associated to an integer partition λ\lambda: that is, λ=⟨λ1,…,λℓ⟩\lambda=\langle\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell}\rangle is a finite nonincreasing sequence of positive integers and Bλ:={(i,j):1≤i≤ℓ,1≤j≤λi}B_{\lambda}:=\{(i,j):1\leq i\leq\ell,1\leq j\leq\lambda_{i}\}. For example, in the case of the staircase partition δn:=⟨n−1,n−2,…,2,1⟩\delta_{n}:=\langle n-1,n-2,\ldots,2,1\rangle, one has that

Rk​(Bδn)=S⁡(n,n−k)R_{k}(B_{\delta_{n}})=S(n,n-k)

is a Stirling number of the second kind [20, §5]. In general, two partitions λ,μ\lambda,\mu are said to be rook equivalent if Rk​(Bλ)=Rk​(Bμ)R_{k}(B_{\lambda})=R_{k}(B_{\mu}) for all kk [12]. This condition can be phrased in various ways; for our purposes, the most convenient characterization [8, Cor. 3.2] is that λ\lambda and μ\mu are rook equivalent if and only if dm​(λ)=dm​(μ)d_{m}(\lambda)=d_{m}(\mu) for all mm, where the dmd_{m} are the diagonal counts

dm​(ν):=|{(i,j)∈Bν:i+j=m+1}|.d_{m}(\nu):=|\{(i,j)\in B_{\nu}:i+j=m+1\}|. (1)

In [10], Garsia and Remmel introduced a qq-analogue of the rook number. This analogue is in terms of the inversion number, defined as follows: given a rook placement ww on a Ferrers board BλB_{\lambda}, for each rook (a,b)∈w(a,b)\in w, delete from BλB_{\lambda} all elements (i,b)(i,b) with i≤ai\leq a and (a,j)(a,j) with j≤bj\leq b; the inversion number inv⁡(w)\operatorname{inv}(w) is the number of undeleted cells. Then the (Garsia–Remmel) qq-rook number of rank kk is

Rk​(λ,q):=∑w​ a placement ofk rooks on ​Bλqinv⁡(w).R_{k}(\lambda;q):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\text{ a placement of}\\ \text{$k$ rooks on }B_{\lambda}\end{subarray}}q^{\operatorname{inv}(w)}.

By definition, Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) is a polynomial in the formal variable qq with nonnegative integer coefficients such that Rk​(λ,1)=Rk​(Bλ)R_{k}(\lambda;1)=R_{k}(B_{\lambda}). For example, the rank-33 qq-rook number of the partition ⟨6,5,3,3⟩\langle 6,5,3,3\rangle is q11+4​q10+10​q9+19​q8+27​q7+30​q6+25​q5+15​q4+6​q3+q2q^{11}+4q^{10}+10q^{9}+19q^{8}+27q^{7}+30q^{6}+25q^{5}+15q^{4}+6q^{3}+q^{2}, and the rook placement in Figure 1 is one of the 2525 that contribute to the coefficient of q5q^{5}.

Analogously to the case q=1q=1, one says two partitions are qq-rook equivalent if they have the same qq-rook numbers. Surprisingly, two partitions are rook equivalent if and only if they are qq-rook equivalent [10, p. 257]. In the particular case λ=δn\lambda=\delta_{n}, the polynomial Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) is a qq-Stirling number of the second kind [10, Eq. I.9]; for more on these numbers, see [22, 31] and Remarks 8 and 10 below.

The same polynomials Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) also arise in enumerative linear algebra, when counting matrices of rank kk over a finite field whose nonzero entries all belong to BλB_{\lambda} [18, Thm. 1]; this connection has led to applications in coding theory, since up to a power of qq, the Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) give the weights of certain rank-metric codes (e.g., see [25, 11, 15]). The qq-rook numbers and the related qq-hit numbers have also recently appeared in the expansions of chromatic symmetric functions of graphs corresponding to certain Dyck paths called abelian [1, 7, 23, 16].

Based on an assortment of empirical and circumstantial evidence, Garsia and Remmel conjectured [10, p. 250] that the polynomials Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) always have unimodal sequence of coefficients, i.e., that if

Rk​(λ,q)=aN​qN+aN−1​qN−1+…+a1​q+a0R_{k}(\lambda;q)=a_{N}q^{N}+a_{N-1}q^{N-1}+\ldots+a_{1}q+a_{0}

then for some mm it holds that aN≤aN−1≤⋯≤am+1≤am≥am−1≥⋯≥a1≥a0a_{N}\leq a_{N-1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{m+1}\leq a_{m}\geq a_{m-1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{1}\geq a_{0}. As we now show, it is not difficult to prove the Garsia–Remmel unimodality conjecture for the cases of the maximum and minimum nontrivial numbers of rooks.

Proposition 1.

For every partition λ=⟨λ1,…,λℓ⟩\lambda=\langle\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell}\rangle, Rℓ​(λ,q)R_{\ell}(\lambda;q) is unimodal.

Proof.

In the case of ℓ\ell rooks, there must be one rook in each row. Consider iteratively placing the rooks beginning with the last row. Regardless of how one has placed rooks in rows k+1,…,ℓk+1,\ldots,\ell, there will be λk−(ℓ−k)\lambda_{k}-(\ell-k) legal positions to place a rook in row kk, and the different choices will leave 0,1,…,λk−(ℓ−k)−10,1,\ldots,\lambda_{k}-(\ell-k)-1 inversions in row kk. Consequently

Rℓ(λ;q)=[λℓ]q⋅[λℓ−1−1]q⋯[λ1−(ℓ−1)]qR_{\ell}(\lambda;q)=[\lambda_{\ell}]_{q}\cdot[\lambda_{\ell-1}-1]_{q}\cdots[\lambda_{1}-(\ell-1)]_{q} (2)

where [n]q:=1+q+q2+…+qn−1[n]_{q}:=1+q+q^{2}+\ldots+q^{n-1}. Thus Rℓ​(λ,q)R_{\ell}(\lambda;q) is a product of log-concave polynomials (i.e., polynomials for which the coefficient sequence satisfies ai2≥ai−1​ai+1a_{i}^{2}\geq a_{i-1}a_{i+1}) with nonnegative coefficients and no internal zeros. The family of such polynomials is closed under products [28, Prop. 2], and furthermore every such polynomial is unimodal [28, p. 500]. ∎

Proposition 2.

For every partition λ\lambda, R1​(λ,q)R_{1}(\lambda;q) is unimodal.

Proof.

It is easy to see [8, proof of Cor. 3.2] that

R1​(λ,q)=∑idi​(λ)⋅q|λ|−iR_{1}(\lambda;q)=\sum_{i}d_{i}(\lambda)\cdot q^{|\lambda|-i} (3)

where did_{i} is as in (1) and |λ|=λ1+λ2+⋯+λℓ|\lambda|=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\cdots+\lambda_{\ell} is the size of λ\lambda. This polynomial is unimodal because, taking mm to be the maximum index for which dm=md_{m}=m and fixing a choice of a box (a,m+2−a)(a,m+2-a) that does not belong to the (m+1)(m+1)st diagonal of BλB_{\lambda}, we have that the map

(x,y)↦{(x,y−1) if ​x<a,(x−1,y) if ​x>a(x,y)\mapsto\begin{cases}(x,y-1)&\text{ if }x<a,\\ (x-1,y)&\text{ if }x>a\end{cases}

is an injection from the kkth diagonal of BλB_{\lambda} to the (k−1)(k-1)st for all k>mk>m, and hence dm≥dm+1≥⋯d_{m}\geq d_{m+1}\geq\cdots. ∎

Progress on the general conjecture has been limited. One reason for this is that, although qq-rook numbers of maximum rank are always log-concave (per the proof of Proposition 1), this is not the case for lower-rank qq-rook numbers, as shown in the next example. Thus, the assorted machinery that has been built up (especially in the past decade [2, 4, 3, 5]) to prove log-concavity results is not directly useful here.

Example 3.

One has (either from (3) or by direct examination) that

R1​(⟨4,1⟩,q)=q4+2​q3+q2+q,R_{1}(\langle 4,1\rangle;q)=q^{4}+2q^{3}+q^{2}+q,

which is not log-concave (since a22=1<2=a1⋅a3a_{2}^{2}=1<2=a_{1}\cdot a_{3}).

A second reason that progress on the general conjecture has been limited is that the conjecture is false.

Proposition 4.

The qq-rook number

R2​(⟨10,9,3,2,1⟩,q)R_{2}(\langle 10,9,3,2,1\rangle;q)

is not unimodal.

Proof.

By considering whether or not the cell (ℓ,λℓ)(\ell,\lambda_{\ell}) has a rook, it is easy to see that the qq-rook numbers satisfy the recurrence relation

Rk​(⟨λ1,…,λℓ−1,λℓ⟩,q)=q⋅Rk​(⟨λ1,…,λℓ−1,λℓ−1⟩,q)+Rk−1​(⟨λ1−1,…,λℓ−1−1⟩,q).R_{k}(\langle\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell-1},\lambda_{\ell}\rangle;q)=q\cdot R_{k}(\langle\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell-1},\lambda_{\ell}-1\rangle;q)+{}\\ R_{k-1}(\langle\lambda_{1}-1,\ldots,\lambda_{\ell-1}-1\rangle;q). (4)

(This is a special case of Dworkin’s “deletion-contraction” recurrence for qq-rook numbers [9, Thm. 6.10].) Repeated applications of (4) yield

R2​(⟨10,9,3,2,1⟩,q)\displaystyle R_{2}(\langle 10,9,3,2,1\rangle;q) =q⋅R2​(⟨10,9,3,2⟩,q)+R1​(⟨9,8,2,1⟩,q),\displaystyle=q\cdot R_{2}(\langle 10,9,3,2\rangle;q)+R_{1}(\langle 9,8,2,1\rangle;q),
R2​(⟨10,9,3,2⟩,q)\displaystyle R_{2}(\langle 10,9,3,2\rangle;q) =q2⋅R2​(⟨10,9,3⟩,q)+(1+q)⋅R1​(⟨9,8,2⟩,q),\displaystyle=q^{2}\cdot R_{2}(\langle 10,9,3\rangle;q)+(1+q)\cdot R_{1}(\langle 9,8,2\rangle;q),
and
R2​(⟨10,9,3⟩,q)\displaystyle R_{2}(\langle 10,9,3\rangle;q) =q3⋅R2​(⟨10,9⟩,q)+(1+q+q2)⋅R1​(⟨9,8⟩,q).\displaystyle=q^{3}\cdot R_{2}(\langle 10,9\rangle;q)+(1+q+q^{2})\cdot R_{1}(\langle 9,8\rangle;q).

By (2), we have R2​(⟨10,9⟩,q)=([9]q)2R_{2}(\langle 10,9\rangle;q)=([9]_{q})^{2}, while the various instances of R1R_{1} can be computed from (3). Plugging these values in and simplifying produces

R2​(⟨10,9,3,2,1⟩,q)=q22+3​q21+7​q20+13​q19+18​q18+21​q17+22​q16+20​q15+21​q14+20​q13+17​q12+12​q11+5​q10+4​q9+3​q8+2​q7+q6,R_{2}(\langle 10,9,3,2,1\rangle;q)=q^{22}+3q^{21}+7q^{20}+13q^{19}+18q^{18}+21q^{17}+{}\\ 22q^{16}+20q^{15}+21q^{14}+{}\\ 20q^{13}+17q^{12}+12q^{11}+5q^{10}+4q^{9}+3q^{8}+2q^{7}+q^{6},

which is manifestly non-unimodal. ∎

Remark 5.

The example in Proposition 4 is the smallest partition that has a non-unimodal qq-rook number: we checked by exhaustive computation (carried out in Sage [30], implemented with the simple recursion (4), with base case R0​(λ,q)=q|λ|R_{0}(\lambda;q)=q^{|\lambda|}) that if |λ|≤24|\lambda|\leq 24, then the qq-rook number Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) is unimodal for all kk. The only other partitions of size 2525 with a non-unimodal qq-rook number are rook equivalent to ⟨10,9,3,2,1⟩\langle 10,9,3,2,1\rangle. For larger nn, the number of partitions of nn with non-unimodal qq-rook number in rank 22 grows steadily; for example, there are 6767 rook equivalence classes of partitions of size 4040 with R2R_{2} non-unimodal (out of 11131113 total classes).

Remark 6.

We record here the results of some further computational experiments:

  • •

    The smallest partitions λ\lambda for which R3​(λ,q)R_{3}(\lambda;q) is not unimodal are ⟨14,13,5,4,3,2,1⟩\langle 14,13,5,4,3,2,1\rangle, of size 4242, and the partitions rook equivalent to it. These partitions are also non-unimodal in rank 22.

  • •

    The partitions λ\lambda of size 4343 for which R3​(λ,q)R_{3}(\lambda;q) is not unimodal are ⟨16,12,5,4,3,2,1⟩\langle 16,12,5,4,3,2,1\rangle and the partitions rook equivalent to it. These partitions are unimodal in rank 22.

  • •

    The smallest partitions λ\lambda for which R4​(λ,q)R_{4}(\lambda;q) is not unimodal are ⟨31,17,16,5,4,3,2⟩\langle 31,17,16,5,4,3,2\rangle, of size 7878, and the partitions rook equivalent to it. These partitions are also non-unimodal in rank 22 but are unimodal in rank 33.

  • •

    For the partition ⟨69,67,65,10,9,7,6,5,4,3,2⟩\langle 69,67,65,10,9,7,6,5,4,3,2\rangle of size 247247, R5​(λ,q)R_{5}(\lambda;q) is not unimodal. This partition was found doing an exploratory search with code written with the help of Gemini [13]. We have no reason to believe this is a minimum-size example, but we have not found a smaller one. See Table 1 for similar non-unimodal examples for k=6,7,8,9,10k=6,7,8,9,10. The code for these explorations is available on the arXiv as an ancillary file and a website with a visualization tool for qq-rook numbers is available at https://ahmorales.math.uqam.ca/Animations/qrooks.html.

It seems reasonable to conjecture that for each integer k>1k>1, there is some partition λ\lambda for which Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) is not unimodal. Typically, it seems that when Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) is not unimodal, there is a gap between kk and the number of parts ℓ⁡(λ)\ell(\lambda) of λ\lambda. For example, every partition λ\lambda with less than 100100 boxes for which R2​(λ,q)R_{2}(\lambda;q) is non-unimodal has ℓ⁡(λ)≥5\ell(\lambda)\geq 5. The smallest example with a gap of size 22 is for the non-unimodal polynomial R3​(⟨24,15,14,3,2⟩,q)R_{3}(\langle 24,15,14,3,2\rangle;q). Is Rℓ−1​(λ,q)R_{\ell-1}(\lambda;q) always unimodal?

Remark 7.

In the tables of data they collected in [10, p. 273–274], Garsia and Remmel noted that the coefficients of the total qq-rook number

R⁡(λ,q):=∑k≥0Rk​(λ,q)R(\lambda;q):=\sum_{k\geq 0}R_{k}(\lambda;q)

also appeared to be unimodal. We have verified this for all partitions λ\lambda such that |λ|≤70|\lambda|\leq 70. For the staircase δn\delta_{n}, R⁡(δn,q)R(\delta_{n};q) is the qq-Bell number [32]. Note that R⁡(λ,q)R(\lambda;q) is not necessarily log-concave since R⁡(⟨2,1⟩,q)=1+2​q+q2+q3R(\langle 2,1\rangle;q)=1+2q+q^{2}+q^{3}.

Remark 8.

The qq-Stirling numbers Sq​(n,k)S_{q}(n,k) of the second kind, defined by Sq​(n,k):=Rn−k​(δn,q)S_{q}(n,k):=R_{n-k}(\delta_{n};q), or alternatively by the recurrence

Sq​(n,k)=qk−1​Sq​(n−1,k−1)+[k]q​Sq​(n−1,k)for0<k≤n,Sq​(0,k)=δ0,k,S_{q}(n,k)=q^{k-1}S_{q}(n-1,k-1)+[k]_{q}S_{q}(n-1,k)\quad\text{for}\quad 0<k\leq n,\qquad S_{q}(0,k)=\delta_{0,k}, (5)

were further conjectured to be log-concave by Wachs–White [31, p. 45]. This conjecture was discussed more recently in work of Sagan and Swanson [26, Conj. 7.4], who verified it for 1≤k≤n≤501\leq k\leq n\leq 50. We have checked it for 1≤k≤n≤2501\leq k\leq n\leq 250. See [26, §1.2] for a history of these polynomials.

It follows easily from the recurrence (5) that these qq-Stirling numbers can be obtained from the following evaluation of a complete symmetric polynomial [14]:

Sq​(n,k)=q(k2)​hn−k​([1]q,[2]q,…,[k]q).S_{q}(n,k)=q^{\binom{k}{2}}h_{n-k}([1]_{q},[2]_{q},\ldots,[k]_{q}).

Such complete symmetric functions are instances of Schur functions: hn−k​(x1,…,xk)=sn−k​(x1,…,xk)h_{n-k}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})=s_{n-k}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}). Could the evaluation above be useful to show log-concavity or unimodality of Sq​(n,k)S_{q}(n,k), as in the principal specialization [29, §7.8] of Schur functions [28, Thm. 13], or by exploiting the denormalized Lorentzian property of Schur polynomials [19]?

Remark 9.

For all partitions λ\lambda of size |λ|≤75|\lambda|\leq 75 and all kk, the rank-kk qq-rook number Rk​(Bλ,q)R_{k}(B_{\lambda};q) is log-concave whenever R1​(Bλ,q)R_{1}(B_{\lambda};q) is log-concave (i.e., if the sequence of diagonal lengths di​(λ)d_{i}(\lambda) are log-concave). Could this be true for all λ\lambda? Note that R1​(δn,q)R_{1}(\delta_{n};q) is log-concave, so this is a strengthening of the Wachs–White conjecture mentioned in the previous remark.

Remark 10.

In [27, Cor. 2.6], Sagan showed that the qq-Stirling numbers of the second kind satisfy the following alternative notion of log-concavity:11 1 See also [21] for an analogous result for the shifted polynomials q−(k2)​Sq​(n,k)q^{-\binom{k}{2}}S_{q}(n,k).

Sq​(n,k)2−Sq​(n,k−1)​Sq​(n,k+1)∈ℕ⁡[q].S_{q}(n,k)^{2}-S_{q}(n,k-1)S_{q}(n,k+1)\in\mathbb{N}[q].

Based on calculations for partitions λ\lambda such that |λ|≤50|\lambda|\leq 50, we conjecture that the qq-rook numbers Rk​(λ,q)R_{k}(\lambda;q) satisfy this notion of log-concavity, i.e., that

Rk​(λ,q)2−Rk−1​(λ,q)​Rk+1​(λ,q)∈ℕ⁡[q]R_{k}(\lambda;q)^{2}-R_{k-1}(\lambda;q)R_{k+1}(\lambda;q)\in\mathbb{N}[q]

for all kk and λ\lambda. At q=1q=1, this conjecture is a consequence of [24, Thm. 1]; see [17] for more about log-concavity for the q=1q=1 case.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
